statement: The janggu is an hourglass-shaped, two-headed drum approximately 66 cm long, featuring a wooden body and skin heads mounted on metal hoops tensioned by cords.
The left head (gungpyeon) is constructed from thick cowhide for low bass tones, while the right head (chaepyeon) is made from thinner horsehide or doghide for high treble tones.
The narrow central waist tube of the janggu is called the jorongmok, which regulates and directs the airflow between the two sound chambers.
In court and jeongak classical music, the player strikes the right head with a thin bamboo stick (yeolchae) and plays the left head with the bare left hand.
In folk music, nongak, and janggu dance, the player uses two sticks: the thin bamboo yeolchae for the right head and the round-headed mallet (gungchae) for the left head.
The janggu is regarded as the most representative drum in traditional Korean music and accompanies court music, folk genres, shaman rituals, and stage dances.
Nongak (traditional Korean community band music, dance, and rituals driven by the janggu) was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Dancer Choi Seung-hee adapted the folk janggu dance into a formal modern stage choreography.

statement: The Metropolitan Museum of Art acquired a preserved 19th-century Korean changgo drum, which was manufactured in the 1800s.
A celadon sajanggu (a ceramic-bodied janggu) was crafted during the Goryeo dynasty and is preserved in the National Museum of Korea.
